transcript.text:
"Not working" can mean a few quite different faults on a tumble dryer, so the first job is to pin down which one it is. In rough order of how often I see them, the usual causes are: no power getting to it (socket or plug fuse), something stopping it starting (door not fully clicked shut, a full water container on a condenser dryer, child lock or delay start), a blocked fluff filter making it overheat and cut out the heat, or less often a broken drive belt or motor. A few quick checks that sort these out: 1. Power: plug something else you know works, like a lamp, into the same socket. If that's dead too, check your fuse box. If the socket is fine, switch off and unplug the dryer and swap the 13A fuse in its plug for a known-good one. If the dryer then comes back to life, it was just the fuse.
2. Door: open the door and shut it firmly until it clicks. Most dryers won't start at all if the door switch doesn't register it as closed.
3. Water container (condenser and heat-pump dryers only): empty it and slide it fully back in. A full tank, or one that isn't seated properly, will stop the dryer or prevent it starting.
4. Filters: with the dryer off, clean the fluff filter in the door opening. If yours has a condenser or second filter behind the bottom flap, rinse that as well. Heavy fluff blocks the airflow, the dryer overheats and it cuts the heat or stops. It would also really help to know exactly what happens when you try to use it. Is it completely dead with no lights? Do the lights come on but nothing starts? Does it hum without the drum turning? Or does it tumble but stay cold or stop partway through? That tells me straight away which direction to go.
Lights come on but nothing happens when I press start. No hum or sound at all, drum doesn't turn.

That helps a lot. If the motor were starting and something mechanical was failing, you'd normally hear a hum or a whirr. 1. The door isn't being registered as shut. This is the most common one. The dryer then quietly refuses to start.
2. Something in the controls is blocking the start. This could be delay start or child lock being on, a programme not fully selected, or on a condenser dryer a full or badly seated water tank.
3. The motor isn't starting. Motors have a thermal cut-out that trips if they overheat, often after fluff build-up, or the motor itself may have failed.
4. Less likely: a snapped drive belt on dryers that have a safety switch to stop the motor, or a start button or control board fault. 1. Door catch. Look at the hook on the door and the slot it goes into. If the hook is cracked, bent or loose, or the door shuts without a firm click, the door switch can't register. Press the door firmly shut with your hand flat and press start at the same time. If it then starts, the catch or door switch is the culprit.
2. Display. Press start and watch closely. A flashing light, symbol or code usually means the dryer is telling you why it won't run (door, tank, filter or child lock). If there's a code, tell me what it shows.
3. Rest and reset. Switch off and unplug it for 30 minutes so any thermal cut-out can cool and reset and the electronics clear. Then plug in, pick a simple timed programme and press start. If it works for a while and then stops again, that points to overheating, usually airflow or fluff.
4. Drum by hand. Unplug it, empty it and turn the drum slowly by hand. - Spins very easily with almost no resistance: the belt has probably come off or snapped. - Stiff or stuck: something is jammed or the rollers are worn. If none of that gets it going and the drum feels normal, the fault is most likely the door switch, the motor or the control side. Those need panels removing and electrical testing, so it's better for an engineer. Could you tell me how the drum feels by hand, and whether anything shows on the

Door doesn't click when I shut it, it swings back slightly open. The plastic tongue on the door has snapped off, found the piece on the floor. If I hold the door shut and press start it runs, stops when I let go.

That settles it. The broken plastic tongue on the door is probably the whole fault. That tongue is the door catch: it hooks into the slot on the cabinet, holds the door shut and presses the door switch closed. Without it the door drifts open, the switch drops out and the dryer won't start or stops. The fact that it runs normally when you hold the door shut is the key evidence. It tells us the door switch, motor and controls are all working, so this is a mechanical part, not an electrical one. I'm quite confident (around 90%) the door catch is the likely part. 1. If it's intact with no cracked plastic or a bit of tongue stuck inside, only the catch on the door is involved. If any snapped piece is lodged in there, unplug the dryer and carefully hook it out.
2. Please don't tape, wedge or hold the door shut to run it. Bypassing the latch means the drum can run with the door able to swing open. Gluing the tongue back on rarely lasts either, because it takes a knock every time the door shuts and it gets warm. On most dryers the door catch is a small separate part held into the inner door panel by a couple of screws or clips, so it's often something an owner can replace with the dryer unplugged. On some designs it's part of the door's inner moulding, though, so it's worth checking how yours fits before deciding. Once it's fixed, if the door clicks shut properly but the dryer still won't start, that would point to the door switch. On current evidence I don't expect that. If you tell me the make and model number, I can help you narrow down the right catch to look for.
It's a Hotpoint, about 5 years old. I don't know the model number offhand though.

[Heading: Likely cause: door handle]
No problem. It's still clearly the door catch: the snapped tongue means the door can't latch, and the fact it runs when you hold the door shut tells us the rest of the dryer is fine. It's a mechanical part, not an electrical one. Hotpoint has used several different door and catch designs over the years, so the model number is what tells us which catch fits. Here's how to find it: 1. Open the door and look around the rim of the door opening, on the cabinet frame or the edge of the door itself. You're looking for a white or silver sticker.
2. The model number is usually a mix of letters and numbers near the top of the label. There's often a separate service or serial number as well. If you can, send me both, or just type out everything on the label and I'll pick out the right bits.
3. If you can't see a label there, check the back of the dryer or the inside of the filter flap at the bottom. The original manual or receipt should have it too. Once I have that, I can help you narrow down the right replacement catch and how it's likely to fit. In the meantime it's best not to use the dryer by holding or wedging the door shut. One more thing worth doing while you have the model number to hand. Some older Hotpoint dryers were covered by a manufacturer safety modification programme. A five-year-old machine is quite likely to be newer than the ones affected, but it only takes a minute to put the model and serial number into Hotpoint's online safety checker, or to look on GOV.UK product safety alerts, to be sure.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
ok, I'll go and look inside the door recess for the model number.

[Heading: Likely cause: door handle]
That's the right place to look. The diagnosis stays the same: the snapped tongue is the door catch, and since the dryer runs when you hold the door shut, the rest of it is working. A few tips while you're there:
1. Open the door fully and look all around the rim of the opening, on the cabinet side and on the inner edge of the door. A torch helps, because the sticker can sit low down or be partly covered in fluff.
2. Note everything on the label: the model number, plus any service number or serial number. Hotpoint often prints a separate service code, and that's very useful for matching the right catch. If it's easier, take a photo and type out what it says.
3. If there's nothing in the door recess, try the back of the dryer or behind the bottom filter flap. There's no rush if the label is hard to read or find right now. It can wait, and the receipt or manual will have it too. Until the catch is replaced, it's best not to run the dryer by holding or wedging the door shut.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
